sections.overview: The grey partridge is a plump, ground-living gamebird of European farmland. Once very common and widespread, it has suffered serious declines across most of its range and is now a conservation concern in the UK.
sections.identification: An adult weighs about 390 g with a wing length near 16 cm. The plumage is finely barred grey and brown, with an orange face and throat, chestnut bars on the flanks and a chestnut tail. Males are larger and usually show a U-shaped chestnut patch on the belly; females are duller, with a smaller patch or none.
sections.habitat: It is a resident, sedentary bird of lowland farmland, most frequent on arable land in the breeding season. It needs open fields for feeding by day and dense cover to hide in and nest. Chicks depend on cover and on invertebrates, even on rough grazing on hill farms in north-east England.
sections.diet: Adults eat mainly seeds, grain, leaves, roots and shoots, with cereals important in the warmer months. Chicks, in contrast, need protein and feed on insects, including sawfly larvae in a north-east England study, and aphids.
sections.behavior: A strictly ground-living bird, it spends the non-breeding season in groups called coveys, usually of 6 to 15 birds and sometimes up to 25, often made up of relatives. Members feed and roost together and keep watch for danger. When threatened, the birds run or fly low and fast, and their bodies can look like clods of earth.
sections.reproduction: In the UK there is typically one brood a year, with a very large clutch of 13–16 eggs, sometimes more than 20. The female alone incubates for 23–25 days. The downy chicks leave the nest at once and can fly short distances at about two weeks old. Breeding typically starts at one year of age.
sections.ecology: Birds of prey such as goshawks and sparrowhawks, and ground predators such as foxes, take adults, eggs and chicks, and higher predation lowers nest success and winter survival. The main driver of decline is agricultural intensification, especially the loss of chick food through pesticide and herbicide use. The birds also disperse seeds in their droppings.
sections.conservation: The IUCN lists the species as Least Concern worldwide, but it has declined across Europe. In the UK it is Red-listed: the breeding population was about 37,000 territories in 2016 and fell by 93% between 1967 and 2024. It typically lives about three years once adult, and the oldest ringed bird reached over five.
